report:
**Conclusion: The evidence is mixed, but leans modestly positive — not a clear "yes."**

The biological rationale is sound: statins block CoQ10 synthesis, which may contribute to muscle symptoms. However, clinical trial results conflict:

**Evidence supporting benefit:**
- A 2018 meta-analysis of RCTs found CoQ10 supplementation "ameliorated statin-associated muscle symptoms, such as muscle pain, muscle weakness, muscle cramps, and muscle tiredness" (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/JAHA.118.009835).
- A 2025 meta-analysis reported "an overall significant reduction in muscle pain intensity after CoQ10 supplementation" in patients with existing statin-induced myopathy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12554813/).

**Evidence showing no benefit:**
- The Banach et al. 2015 meta-analysis (6 RCTs, 302 patients) concluded results "do not suggest any significant benefit of CoQ10 supplementation in improving statin-induced myopathy" (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S002561961400799X).
- An RCT of patients with confirmed statin myalgia found no difference: pain reduction occurred in 53% of CoQ10 recipients vs. 65% of placebo recipients (p=0.43) (https://www.atherosclerosis-journal.com/article/S0021-9150(15)01205-8/fulltext).

**Reconciliation:** The earlier meta-analysis (2015) was negative; subsequent meta-analyses incorporating newer trials (2018, 2025) found a statistically significant benefit. The effect appears real but modest, and individual responses vary. Mayo Clinic notes CoQ10 "may help prevent statin side effects in some people" but more studies are needed. The answer is a cautious, qualified "probably, for some patients" rather than a definitive yes.
